translation: Two other small photos with scalloped borders, seemingly dating from the same year, feature the same girl but smaller, in a ruffle dress with balloon sleeves.
In the first one, she's nestled playfully against a woman with a massive figure captured monolithically in a wide-striped dress, her hair rolled up in large coils.
In the other one, she is raising her left fist; her right hand is held by a tall man dressed in light jacket and pleated pants exuding a nonchalant stance.
Both photos were taken on the same day against an unfenced wall mounted by flowerbeds amidst paved courtyard.
A clothesline appears above their heads containing an attached pin left hanging through it.
Another photograph, signed by the same photographer but printed on simpler paper without the gold border—probably intended for the same family distribution—shows a little girl about four years old.
She looks serious, almost sad despite her plump and rosy face under short hair parted in the middle and held back by barrettes with attached ribbons, like butterflies.
Her left hand rests on the same intricately styled Louis XVI table, now fully visible.
Her pudgy arm appears stuffed into her blouse; her overall dress is hiked up in front due to a protruding belly, perhaps an indication of rickets (around 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment and they were considered handsome as soldiers.
On the evening of their military examination, they would tour local cafes to celebrate the glory of being recognized as real men.
Before joining the regiment, they were just kids and held no value in the labor or marriage market.
Afterward, they could have a wife and children.
During leave, their uniforms paraded around the neighborhood endowed them with patriotic beauty and potential sacrifice.
The shadow of victorious fighters such as GIs hovered around them.
The rough fabric of their uniform jackets, brushed when someone tip-toed to embrace them, marked an absolute division between men's world and women's world.
Seeing them invoked a sense of heroism.

Beneath the stillness, last year's circus posters with a photo of Roger Lanzac, first communion pictures distributed to friends, and the Club des Chansonniers on Radio Luxembourg filled the days with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, people would crowd around the window of the general electric store to watch television.
Cafes began investing in their own sets to draw in customers.
Dirt-bike tracks wound along the hillsides and one could watch deafening vehicles all day long rise and fall along them.
The growing impatience of commerce with its new buzzwords "initiative", "dynamism", shook up daily life in towns.
Between a fairground and a village festival, Commercial Fortnight took hold as a springtime ritual.
In town center streets loudspeakers bellowed out encouragements to buy interspersed with songs by Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine for chances to win either a Simca car or dining room set.
On stage at City Hall square, a local host cracked jokes by Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard while rallying candidates for Sing it or Leave it or Double or Quits just like on radio shows.
Seated in one corner of the dais under her crown was Queen Commerce herself.
Goods moved forward in festive colors.
People used phrases such as "times are changing" or "you can't just get stuck in your ways you go dumb just staying at home".
But they only spoke of what they had seen, which could be relived through eating and drinking.
They didn't have enough talent or conviction to talk about what they knew but hadn't seen.
Therefore, it was not about Jewish children boarding trains for Auschwitz, nor the starving dead picked up in the Warsaw ghetto in the morning, nor the 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima.

Hence this impression that teaching history lessons, documentaries and films later would not dispel: neither the crematory ovens nor atomic bombs were part of the same era as black market butter, air raid warnings and trips to the basement.
They compared it to the previous war, the Great one, that of '14, which had been won with blood and glory a real man's war that the women at the table listened to with respect.
They spoke of the Chemin des Dames and Verdun, of gas victims, and of hearing church bells ring on November 11th 1918.
They named villages from which not a single young soldier sent to fight at the front had returned.
They contrasted soldiers in muddy trenches to prisoners taken in '40 who spent five warm sheltered years without even encountering any bomb shelling above their heads.
They argued about heroism and misfortune.

The children didn't listen and hurried to leave the table as soon as they were allowed, taking advantage of the general goodwill of holidays to partake in forbidden games, jump on beds and swing upside down.
But they remembered everything.
Beside the fabulous time which they would not order for a long time the collapse, exodus, occupation, landing victory found dull these nameless days where they were growing up.
They regretted not having been born or barely born when it was necessary to go in cohort on roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
From this unexperienced time, there persisted a tenacious regret.
The memories shared by others infused them with a secret nostalgia for this era that they had missed by so little and filled them with hope that one day they will live through such times themselves.
The frenzy that had followed the Liberation was fading.
Then, people only thought about going out and the world was full of desires to be satisfied immediately.
Anything that constituted a first since the war aroused a rush, bananas, National Lottery tickets, fireworks.

By entire neighborhoods, from the grandmother supported by her daughters to the newborn in a stroller, people rushed to the fairgrounds, torchlight processions and at Bouglione Circus where they almost got trampled in hurly-burly.
They flocked prayerfully and singing along roadsides to welcome Our Lady of Boulogne statue and escort it through kilometers on following day.
Whether secular or religious, any occasion was just right for them to be outdoors together as if they wanted to continue living collectively.
Sunday evening saw busses return from beach with lads clamoring too loudly atop luggage racks while wearing shorts.
Dogs roamed freely around town mating on street corners right before every eyesight.
Family narrative and social narrative are one and the same.

The voices of the guests defined the areas of their youth: the countryside and farms where, from lost memory, men had been laborers and girls maidservants; the factory where they all met, mingled, and married; the small businesses where the most ambitious had risen.

They drew stories with no personal events other than births, marriages, and deaths—no travels except for military service in a far-off garrison town—existences occupied by work, its hardness and weariness, threats from alcohol.
School was a mythical backdrop—a brief golden age—with a hard-nosed Teacher as its god wielding an iron ruler to rap knuckles.
The browned photos with their backs stained by all the fingers that had held them at other meals a mix of coffee and grease fused into an indistinguishable colour were passed from hand to hand.
In the stiff and serious newlyweds, guests of the wedding ranged in several rows along a wall, one recognized neither their parents nor anyone else.
Neither was it oneself seen in the half-naked baby of indistinct sex on a cushion but rather someone else, a creature belonging to a silent and inaccessible time.
